14.text: Primitive magic performances include certain acts, and utterances of

15.text: verbal formulas which tend to acquire an established text that is learned by

16.text: heart. A verbal formula with its prescribed act forms an incantation, and

17.text: one is rarely used without the other. An incantation is thought to increase

18.text: the mysterious force of an amulet and make it more permanent. The Koryak

19.text: give expression to this idea by calling their amulets “fixed by an incantation”

25.text: In selecting amulets, primitive man is not satisfied with objects as

26.text: they present themselves to him naturally. Actuated by a general desire to

27.text: accentuate the anthropomorphous qualities of the objects of his veneration, he

28.text: very early undertakes to improve them with his own hand and to give them

29.text: a human-like form. In this, however, he does not go beyond the first steps,

30.text: because the power of a belief once established hinders further innovation.

34.text: We find among the Chukchee both classes of amulets, — those of

35.text: natural shape, and those worked up by man. To the first class belong

36.text: stones, pieces of bone, and other objects, which are picked up under various

37.text: circumstances, as was said before. For purposes of divination, stones are

38.text: generally used, as will be explained in Chapter XV. Amulets of animal

39.text: provenience belong to the same class. These may consist of dried skins, or

40.text: be represented by a small part of a skin, by a skull, by the tip of the nose,

41.text: by a single claw, or by a tuft of hair. A bird is represented by a feather.
